analysis.methods: PA and NA sequences were obtained and linked to the clinical cohort for mutation-clinical outcome analyses.
analysis.main_results: Among 765 inpatients with influenza A virus infection, the median age was 68 years; 5.0% were severe disease and 9.9% died. Major high-level resistance mutations were absent; detected NA/PA mutations showed no robust association with severe disease or mortality. PA-F105L showed an exploratory association with longer LOS, but this finding was attenuated after adjustment and was confounded by clade and calendar period.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Clinical outcomes were driven mainly by host factors and admission severity.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: Multiple testing was addressed by controlling the false discovery rate using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. The supplied evidence does not report any specific limitations related to the study design or population.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to investigate the association between specific neuraminidase (NA) and polymerase acidic (PA) mutations and clinical outcomes in hospitalized adults with influenza A virus infection. Conducted at Ruijin Hospital in Shanghai between 2019 and 2024, the study analyzed 765 patients with RT-PCR-confirmed influenza A. The findings revealed that older age, higher CURB-65 score, and bacterial/fungal co-infection were the main correlates of mortality, while antiviral regimen and Ct value were not independently associated with mortality or severe outcomes. Although some mutations showed an exploratory association with prolonged length of stay, these findings were confounded by clade and calendar period. The study concluded that clinical outcomes were primarily driven by host factors and admission severity, and that the associations between NA/PA mutations and outcomes require further validation.

title: Population attributable mortality associated with respiratory viruses in Ontario, Canada: a population-based ecological analysis

analysis.research_question_and_background: Respiratory viruses are major contributors to population mortality, but cause-of-death coding undercounts their impact. The study aimed to estimate the population attributable fraction of mortality associated with specific respiratory viruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: An ecological analysis was conducted using monthly all-cause mortality data in Ontario, Canada, from January 1993 to February 2025. The study focused on influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.methods: Negative binomial models with secular trends, Fourier seasonal terms, and population offsets were used to analyze mortality data. Sensitivity analyses examined different temporal stratifications and modeling approaches.
analysis.main_results: Pre-pandemic, influenza A accounted for 1.8% (95% CI 1.4–2.3%) of mortality, while influenza B showed no detectable impact. Over the combined pandemic period, SARS-CoV-2 accounted for 6.1% (95% CI 4.2–8.0%) of deaths, which was approximately 4-fold higher than pre-pandemic influenza A burden.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study found that SARS-CoV-2 was associated with a significantly higher population mortality burden than seasonal influenza A, despite the availability of countermeasures.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the continued importance of respiratory virus prevention strategies, as post-PHEIC data suggest that the mortality burden from respiratory viruses has not returned to pre-pandemic levels.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's estimates for influenza A and RSV were sensitive to seasonal adjustment, indicating potential variability in results based on modeling choices. The evidence strength is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to estimate the population attributable fraction (PAF) of mortality associated with influenza A and B, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 in Ontario, Canada, from 1993 to 2025. Using ecological regression models, the research found that pre-pandemic influenza A accounted for 1.8% of mortality, while influenza B had no detectable impact. During the pandemic period, SARS-CoV-2 was associated with a 6.1% PAF, which was approximately 4-fold higher than pre-pandemic influenza A. Sensitivity analyses revealed that results for influenza A and RSV were sensitive to seasonal adjustment, suggesting the importance of modeling choices. The study highlights the continued public health significance of respiratory virus prevention strategies, as post-PHEIC data indicate that mortality burdens have not returned to pre-pandemic levels.

title: Immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine in adults living with HIV compared with HIV-uninfected adults: a study from China

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults living with HIV compared with HIV-uninfected adults, addressing the knowledge gap about how HIV affects vaccine responses in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study was a single-center, open-label comparative analysis derived from a larger three-arm clinical study conducted in Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China. It included 236 adults living with HIV (Group 1) and 236 age- and sex-comparable HIV-uninfected adults (Group 2).
analysis.methods: Immunogenicity was assessed using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) antibody testing against A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains, with blood samples collected before and 28 days after vaccination. Safety was evaluated by monitoring adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) during 6 months of follow-up.
analysis.main_results: At 28 days post-vaccination, seroconversion rates did not differ significantly between Group 1 and Group 2 for A(H1N1), but were significantly lower in Group 1 for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria (all P < 0.001). Post-vaccination GMTs were also significantly lower in Group 1 for all three strains. Most AEs were mild, and no Grade 4 adverse reactions or vaccine-related SAEs were reported.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that adults living with HIV developed substantial antibody responses following IIV3 vaccination, although the magnitude of response varied across influenza strains, particularly for A(H3N2).
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that IIV3 is safe and well tolerated in adults living with HIV, supporting current recommendations for influenza vaccination in this population, and highlight the need for further research on strain-specific immune responses in HIV-positive individuals.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's limitations include the use of clinical symptoms to identify influenza-like illness (ILI) without virological confirmation, which precludes assessing vaccine efficacy. The evidence is moderate due to the observational nature of the analysis and the lack of virological confirmation for ILI.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated the immunogenicity and safety of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine (IIV3) in adults living with HIV compared to HIV-uninfected adults in China. The research aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding vaccine responses in HIV-positive individuals. A total of 489 participants were enrolled, with 237 in the HIV group and 252 in the uninfected group. Immunogenicity was measured using hemagglutination inhibition (HI) assays against A(H1N1), A(H3N2), and B/Victoria strains, while safety was assessed through monitoring adverse events. Results showed that seroconversion rates for A(H1N1) were similar between groups, but significantly lower for A(H3N2) and B/Victoria in the HIV group. Post-vaccination GMTs were also lower in the HIV group for all three strains. Most adverse events were mild, and no serious adverse events were reported. The authors concluded that adults living with HIV developed substantial antibody responses to IIV3, though the magnitude varied by strain. The study supports current vaccination recommendations for HIV-positive adults but has limitations due to the lack of virological confirmation for ILI, which affects the assessment of vaccine efficacy. The evidence is moderate in strength.

title: Complementing Biosafety Levels With Societal Safety Levels

analysis.research_question_and_background: Biosafety level (BSL) classifications of biological agents have succeeded at minimizing occupational risk inside laboratories, but largely neglect the potential for onward transmission. The study addresses the need for a framework that considers societal safety in addition to laboratory biosafety.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a conceptual and policy analysis proposing the use of Societal Safety Levels (SSLs) for laboratory research involving replication-competent potential pandemic pathogens. It does not involve empirical data collection or specific populations.
analysis.methods: SSLs are formalized based on expected public fatalities per year, calculated from (i) estimated probability of laboratory release, (ii) likelihood of societal transmission, and (iii) consequence. The methods focus on quantifying societal harm thresholds for pandemic-capable pathogens.
analysis.main_results: We find that applying the 0.1 expected deaths per facility-year standard common across multiple major-hazard industries to potential pandemic pathogen research would require marked safety improvements.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that complementing BSLs with SSLs would establish enforceable accident-safety thresholds for pandemic-capable pathogens, aligning high-risk biological research with quantitative safety standards used in other hazardous industries.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings can inform the development of a more comprehensive safety framework for pandemic-capable pathogens, enhancing public health preparedness and risk management.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on conceptual analysis and does not involve empirical data collection, which limits the strength of the evidence. However, the proposed framework is grounded in existing safety standards and is considered to have moderate evidence strength.

analysis.summary_en: This study proposes the introduction of Societal Safety Levels (SSLs) to complement existing Biosafety Levels (BSLs) for laboratory research involving replication-competent potential pandemic pathogens. The authors argue that BSLs primarily focus on minimizing occupational risk but neglect the societal implications of pathogen release. They suggest that SSLs, based on expected public fatalities per year, could provide enforceable thresholds for accident safety, aligning high-risk biological research with quantitative safety standards used in other hazardous industries. The study highlights the need for marked safety improvements in pandemic-capable pathogen research, using a standard common across major-hazard industries. While the analysis is conceptual, it offers a novel approach to balancing laboratory safety with public health risk management. The proposed framework may inform future policy development and enhance public health preparedness.

title: Comparative immunogenicity of several inactivated influenza vaccines among healthcare workers in Hong Kong

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to compare the immunogenicity of three licensed egg-based inactivated influenza vaccines among healthcare workers in Hong Kong during the 2025/26 season to address the need for understanding vaccine effectiveness in this population.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Age- and sex-matched recipients (n=30-40 per group) with paired pre- and post-vaccination sera were identified from an ongoing cohort.
analysis.methods: Hemagglutination-inhibition assays were performed against the egg-propagated 2025/26 vaccine reference strains.
analysis.main_results: The three vaccines induced broadly comparable geometric mean fold-rises, post-vaccination geometric mean titers, proportions achieving titers >=40, and seroconversion rates against vaccine strains.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These real-world data support the interchangeability of the three products for seasonal influenza vaccination programs among healthcare workers.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide specific implications for the selection and interchangeability of inactivated influenza vaccines in seasonal vaccination programs targeting healthcare workers.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on real-world data from a single cohort, but the evidence is strong due to the direct comparison of immunogenicity parameters across the three vaccines.

analysis.summary_en: This study compared the immunogenicity of three egg-based inactivated influenza vaccines—TetrAnflu, Fluarix Tetra, and Vaxigrip—among healthcare workers in Hong Kong during the 2025/26 season. The research aimed to address the need for understanding vaccine effectiveness in this population. Age- and sex-matched recipients with paired pre- and post-vaccination sera were identified from an ongoing cohort. Hemagglutination-inhibition assays were conducted against the egg-propagated 2025/26 vaccine reference strains. The results showed that all three vaccines induced comparable geometric mean fold-rises, post-vaccination geometric mean titers, proportions achieving titers >=40, and seroconversion rates against vaccine strains. These findings support the interchangeability of the vaccines in seasonal influenza vaccination programs for healthcare workers. The study provides relevant data for vaccine selection and use in this group. However, the evidence is based on a single cohort, which may limit generalizability.
